Published in final edited form as: Gastrointest Endosc Clin N Am. 2012 Aug 20;22(4):661–677. doi: 10.1016/j.giec.2012.07.004 Introduction In this chapter we review issues related to identifying the appropriate patient to test for celiac disease (CD), the performance characteristics of serological testing, the role of gene testing for Human Leukocyte Antigen DQ2 and DQ8 haplotypes, and issues related to the performance of small intestinal biopsy. The chapter concludes with a review of special diagnostic considerations in pediatric patients. Identifying the Appropriate Patient to Test for Celiac Disease Diagnoses of CD are increasing in the United States and worldwide. In a population-based study of individuals in Olmsted County, MN, the annual incidence of CD increased dramatically from 0.9 per 100,000 individuals in the years prior to the availability of serological tests (1950–1989) to 9.1 per 100,000 in the years 2000–2001.1 Analysis of claims data from a national insurance company found that diagnoses of CD continued to increase through the year 2003, the last year of the analysis.2 Despite evidence of increasing rates of diagnosis, the majority of patients in the United States remain undiagnosed. Population based data are sparse, but inferences on the ratio of undiagnosed-to-diagnosed individuals can be made based on what is known regarding the seroprevalence of CD in the general population (0.8–1%).3–5 In 2001, the point prevalence of diagnosed CD in Olmsted County was 0.04%.1 If the seroprevalence of CD is 0.8%, then approximately 95% of patients with CD were undiagnosed at that time. While diagnosis rates are increasing, the fact that the seroprevalence of CD is also increasing4, 6 may result in a persistently high undiagnosed-to-diagnosed ratio. The high fraction of undiagnosed patients in the United States stands in contrast to parts of Europe, including Italy and Finland, in which the threshold to test for CD is lower and so the fraction of diagnosed patients is substantially higher.7–8 One approach to address the relatively low rates of CD diagnosis in the United States is to institute a program of population screening, in which all individuals regardless of symptoms undergo serological testing for CD, and those who screen positive subsequently undergo esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) with small intestinal biopsy. Advocates for this approach note that CD meets World Health Organization criteria for diseases that warrant mass screening: early clinical detection is difficult; the condition is common; screening tests are highly sensitive and specific; effective treatment is available; and untreated disease can lead to complications.9 Given the reduction in mortality risk that occurs in the years after diagnosis and institution of the gluten-free diet10 and the reduced health care expenditures after diagnosis of CD,2 screening for CD may be cost effective, and was found to be so in to three quantitative analyses.11–13 Despite calls for general population screening, problems with this approach have led to targeted case finding as the preferred method of increasing diagnosis rates. Apart from unresolved questions regarding the logistics of screening (such as deciding on the appropriate age and interval of screening) limitations of the currently available serological tests pose a significant problem. Given that the prevalence of CD in the general population is 1%, any test with an imperfect specificity will result in a large number of false-positives. Assuming that the specificity of tissue transglutaminase (TTG) IgA is 98%,14 its positive predictive value when employed in the general population is only 34%; as a result, two thirds of screened individuals who have a positive result will undergo EGD with biopsy and not be diagnosed with CD; this false-positive rate may be reduced by only performing a biopsy on patients with dual positive serologies of TTG endomysial antibody (EMA), but difficulties with the latter serology (see below, Serological and Genetic Testing) makes this approach less than ideal. In addition to the technical limitations of serological screening and its attendant false positive rate, one objection to routine screening for CD is based on the persistent uncertainty regarding the long-term prognosis of asymptomatic, undiagnosed CD. A major argument for screening is that CD is associated with an increased mortality risk, which declines in the years following diagnosis,10 a decline that is attributed to the protective effects of the gluten-free diet. The evidence for a mortality risk in undiagnosed CD is less consistent. In an analysis of thawed serum, Rubio-Tapia, et al identified individuals with positive CD serologies (both TTG and EMA) in 14 out of 9,133 (0.2%) participants in the Warren Air Force cohort.4 With a follow-up period of 45 years, the patients with seropositivity (who all remained undiagnosed) had a nearly four-fold risk of death compared to seronegative individuals (HR 3.9; 95% CI 2.0–7.5). In a second cohort study, healthy volunteers with a positive TTG had an increased mortality compared to seronegative subjects (HR 2.53; 95% CI 1.50–4.25).15 But in four other studies in England,16 Finland,17 Ireland,18 and individuals older than 50 in Olmsted county,19 no increase in mortality was noted in undiagnosed seropositive individuals as compared to their seronegative counterparts. A recent meta-analysis found a modestly increased mortality risk in patients with CD based on serology alone (OR 1.16; 95% CI 1.02–1.31),20 but this pooled analysis included seropositive patients who underwent small intestinal biopsy that was normal,10 raising the possibility of confounding by indication. My name is Melissa Snyder, and I am the co-director of the Antibody Immunology Laboratory at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. I’m so glad you are able to join me for a brief review of published guidelines for the diagnosis of celiac disease, with a specific focus on the role of laboratory testing. Disclosures Before beginning the presentation, I will disclose that I have served as a member of the Strategic Advisory Committee for Werfen, which is an in vitro diagnostic company that manufactures and sells kits for celiac serology testing. Introduction to celiac disease Celiac disease is caused by an inflammatory response by the patient’s own immune system, leading to damage of the small intestinal villi. The figure to the left shows a biopsy of a normal small intestine with intact villae. The middle and right-most figures represent the partial and total villous atrophy that can occur in celiac disease. Celiac disease develops in an individual having both the genetic susceptibility and the proper environmental exposure. The environmental exposure is dietary gluten, a cereal grain protein from wheat, barley, and rye. The genetic component are specific alleles of the human leukocyte antigen complex, namely HLA-DQ2 and HLA-DQ8. Diagnosis of celiac disease The evaluation of a patient for suspected celiac disease includes a review of clinical symptoms and co-existing conditions; an intestinal biopsy with evidence of villous atrophy; serology testing for endomysial, tissue transglutaminase, and deamidated gliadin antibodies; and evaluation for the genetic risk factors including family history and presence of HLA-DQ2/DQ8. Treatment for celiac disease is implementation of a gluten-free diet. The goal of this treatment is to remove the inciting antigen. With a successful gluten-free diet, the patient should begin to see resolution of their clinical symptoms, which is often accompanied by reconstitution of the intestinal villae and conversion to a negative serology. For a more in-depth review of diagnostic tests for celiac disease and the algorithms offered through Mayo Clinic Laboratories, I will refer you to the Hot Topic “Diagnostic Testing Algorithms for Celiac Disease.” Published guidelines Since 2005, a number of diagnostic guidelines for celiac disease have been published by various professional organizations throughout the world. The guidelines are listed in this table in chronological order by publication date, although I want to point out that in 2020, the European Society for Pediatric Gastroenterology, Hepatology and Nutrition published an update to their original paper, which was published in 2012. With the exception of the pediatric gastroenterology societies, all other guidelines focus primarily on adults, although most also highlight specific aspects of testing that would be relevant for children. Given the large number of published guidelines, it isn’t possible during this “Hot Topic” to review each in detail. Rather, I will focus on aspects of testing where there is general agreement across the various organizations, as well as instances where there is a lack of consensus. If you are interested in further details, the references for each guideline are included in this slide. Who should be tested for celiac disease? The first aspect of testing considered by all the guidelines is who should be tested. There is agreement that testing is indicated for certain symptomatic and asymptomatic persons. Symptomatic patients are those who have evidence of clinical symptoms that could be associated with celiac disease. In comparison, asymptomatic individuals would be those persons who have no appreciable clinical symptoms but are at higher risk for developing celiac disease in comparison to the general population. In terms of symptoms, most guidelines consider both classical and nonclassical manifestations. These lists are not exhaustive, and there are subtle differences between the guidelines; however, most guidelines include diarrhea, weight loss, bloating, iron-deficient anemia, cachexia, and edema as classical symptoms, while nonclassical symptoms include abdominal pain and distension, constipation, vomiting, delayed puberty, amenorrhea, chronic fatigue, and hypertransaminasemia. Elevated liver enzymes is highlighted by several guidelines as one of the more common incidental lab findings which should prompt an evaluation for undiagnosed celiac disease. Moving now to asymptomatic individuals, we find that most guidelines advocate for testing in first-degree relatives of patients with celiac disease and for patients who have been diagnosed with other autoimmune diseases, such as type I diabetes or autoimmune thyroid disease. Some guidelines also identify persons with selective IgA deficiency, as this phenotype occurs more frequently in patients with celiac disease compared to the general population. Lastly, individuals with certain chromosomal abnormalities, such as Down syndrome or Turner syndrome, should be considered for testing even in the absence of obvious clinical symptoms. How to test for celiac disease? Serology Next, we will look at what the guidelines suggest on how to test, and we will begin with serology. fetched_contents.text: Diagnosis of Celiac Disease This procedure takes a little less than thirty minutes and, for adults, sedatives and local anesthetics are used. Children are usually put under general anesthesia. During the biopsy, the gastroenterologist will insert a small tube with a camera through the patient’s mouth and into the digestive tract to the small intestine. Once there, the physician will examine the duodenum (entryway into the small intestine) and take multiple tissue samples due to the “patchy” nature of villous atrophy. The tissue samples will then be examined by a pathologist under a microscope and assigned a Marsh classification. Since there are no nerve endings in the lining of the intestine, the procedure is not painful – though some patients may experience a sore throat. Patients who cannot or will not tolerate an endoscopy may be given the option to undergo video capsule or “pill” endoscopy where a capsule the size of a large vitamin pill is swallowed and takes thousands of pictures of the small intestine. However, there is no conclusive evidence that this can substitute for traditional endoscopy and biopsy.

## Branch report: patient symptoms and how they relate to celiac disease

### Which symptoms are consistent with celiac disease?

The evidence clearly identifies several symptoms commonly associated with celiac disease. Classical symptoms include diarrhea, weight loss, bloating, and iron-deficient anemia [N2-F2]. Non-classical symptoms include abdominal pain and distension, constipation, vomiting, delayed puberty, amenorrhea, chronic fatigue, and hypertransaminasemia [N2-F2]. The Mayo Clinic also notes that intestinal damage often causes symptoms such as diarrhea, fatigue, weight loss, bloating, or anemia [N3-R1]. In addition, non-classical celiac disease can present with mild gastrointestinal symptoms without clear signs of malabsorption [N3-R2]. This means that fatigue and mild GI symptoms are not unique to celiac disease, but they can still be relevant if they are part of a broader clinical picture.

### Which symptoms are more suggestive of other diagnoses?

The evidence also emphasizes that celiac disease can be confused with other gluten-related disorders or unrelated conditions. The evidence explicitly states that celiac disease is often confused with non-celiac gluten sensitivity (NCGS) or wheat allergy [N3-R4]. This is important because it means that mild GI symptoms and fatigue can also be explained by other diagnoses, rather than celiac disease itself. The broader context from the diagnosis pathway further supports that endoscopy and biopsy remain the gold standard for confirmation [N4-F3]. In other words, symptoms alone are not enough to distinguish celiac disease from other conditions.

### How fatigue and mild GI symptoms affect diagnostic confidence?

Fatigue and mild GI symptoms affect diagnostic confidence in two ways. First, they are compatible with celiac disease, especially in the non-classical presentation described in the evidence [N3-R2]. Second, they are not sufficiently specific to support a confident diagnosis on their own. The same evidence notes that celiac disease can be confused with other gluten-related disorders and that the serological tests have low diagnostic accuracy if used alone [N1-R3]. This means that while the patient’s symptoms are plausible for celiac disease, they are not sufficient to justify immediate gluten-free treatment without further testing.

### Bottom line for the patient

From the evidence, fatigue and mild GI symptoms are consistent with celiac disease but are not enough on their own to confirm it [N2-F2][N3-R1][N3-R2]. The patient should be treated as a possible celiac candidate, but the presence of these symptoms alone does not mean the diagnosis is certain [N3-R4]. The best next step is to move toward diagnostic testing rather than relying on symptoms alone [N4-F3].

## Branch report: whether borderline serology supports a gluten-free diet

### How likely true celiac disease is with borderline serology

The evidence strongly suggests that borderline serology is not a strong indicator of true celiac disease. The National Celiac Association states that a simple gliadin antibody test can be elevated in many conditions and should not be ordered on its own [N1-R3]. The broader diagnostic review also notes that serological testing has limited performance characteristics and that false positives can occur even with “borderline” results [N1-F1]. In other words, borderline serology increases the possibility of a false positive rather than confirming a true diagnosis.

### What factors increase or reduce the threshold for diagnosis

Several factors affect the threshold for diagnosis. The Mayo Clinic guidelines emphasize that TTG-IgA is the optimal initial test, and it should be used with total IgA to avoid false-negative results in IgA deficiency [N2-F2]. This means that the diagnostic threshold is not low; it is higher when the test is done properly with appropriate adjuncts. The review also explains that the positive predictive value of serology in the general population is low because of the high prevalence of undiagnosed celiac disease and imperfect specificity [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means that the threshold for acting on a borderline result should be higher than on a clearly positive result. The evidence also supports a targeted approach rather than universal screening, especially when serology is borderline [N1-F1].

### Whether a gluten-free trial is defensible or should be delayed

A gluten-free trial is defensible only when the diagnostic uncertainty is high enough that the potential benefits of early treatment outweigh the risks of misdiagnosis. The evidence explicitly warns that an incorrect diagnosis of celiac disease represents a major health risk because of the necessity of a lifelong gluten-free diet [N5-R2]. It also says that if a gluten-free diet has been started, celiac antibody blood testing is not accurate [N5-R1]. This matters because a trial can destroy the diagnostic value of subsequent serology and biopsy.

The guidelines also note that gluten challenge is most commonly used when gluten intake has already been reduced or eliminated before definitive evaluation [N2-R2]. That means a gluten-free trial can be useful only in a narrow, well-defined setting. For borderline serology, the evidence suggests it should be delayed rather than used as the first step [N1-R3][N1-F1]. In other words, the safest approach is to prioritize endoscopy and biopsy first, and to reserve a gluten-free trial only after diagnostic testing has been completed or only in the very rare case where the clinical benefit of immediate treatment clearly outweighs the diagnostic risk [N2-F2][N5-R2].

### Bottom line for the patient

Borderline serology does not strongly support a gluten-free diet because it is not specific and can be misleading [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The threshold for diagnosis should be higher than for a clearly positive result, and the evidence supports using TTG-IgA with total IgA as the best initial approach [N2-F2]. A gluten-free trial is defensible only when the diagnostic uncertainty is very high and the risk of misdiagnosis is unacceptable, but in the current context, it should be delayed rather than used immediately [N5-R2][N5-R1]. The patient should be advised that a lifelong gluten-free diet is a major commitment and should not be assumed without stronger evidence [N5-R2].

## Branch report: practical risks of gluten-free trial and diagnostic delay

### What diagnostic information can be lost by starting a gluten-free diet

The most important diagnostic loss is the loss of meaningful serology. The evidence explicitly states that antibody blood testing is not accurate if the patient is already on a gluten-free diet [N5-R1]. It also notes that gluten challenge is used when gluten intake has already been reduced or eliminated before definitive evaluation, which implies that the trial can interfere with the diagnostic process rather than support it [N2-R2]. In addition, the evidence on celiac screening says that if a gluten-free diet has been started, celiac disease antibody blood testing is not accurate [N5-R1]. This means that starting a gluten-free diet can erase the very evidence needed to confirm or rule out celiac disease.

Biopsy and endoscopy are the gold standard, but they still depend on the patient having active gluten exposure. The diagnostic pathway notes that endoscopy with biopsy is the first choice and the gold standard for diagnosing and confirming celiac disease [N4-F3]. The review also explains that endoscopy findings can be helpful and that a no-biopsy approach can reduce cost and risk, but it does not substitute for traditional endoscopy and biopsy [N4-R4][N4-F3]. This means that diagnostic delay can still be reasonable if the patient is kept on gluten and scheduled for endoscopy, but starting a gluten-free diet removes that window.

### When a trial is useful and when it is misleading

A trial is useful only in a very limited setting. The evidence says gluten challenge is most commonly employed when gluten intake has already been reduced or eliminated before a definitive diagnostic evaluation [N2-R2]. That means a trial is useful if the patient is already on a gluten-free diet and the clinician wants to reassess the diagnosis, not as a first step in a patient with borderline serology. The evidence also emphasizes that serology can be misleading, especially when used alone [N1-R3][N1-F1], which means a trial is misleading if used in place of proper diagnostic testing.

The evidence further cautions that an incorrect diagnosis of celiac disease represents a major health risk because of the lifelong gluten-free diet [N5-R2]. This is a powerful reason to avoid a trial unless the diagnostic burden is extremely high. In borderline serology, the evidence supports a targeted approach rather than a trial-first strategy [N1-F1]. In other words, a trial is useful only when the patient has already been exposed to gluten and the diagnostic pathway has been partially completed; otherwise, it is misleading and harmful.

### How to minimize harm while waiting for testing

To minimize harm while waiting for testing, the evidence supports keeping the patient on gluten and scheduling endoscopy and biopsy as soon as possible [N4-F3]. The Mayo Clinic guidelines also note that TTG-IgA should be used with total IgA to help identify IgA deficiency and avoid false-negative results [N2-F2]. This means the safest waiting strategy is to follow the recommended diagnostic pathway, including appropriate serology and genetic testing if indicated, rather than starting a gluten-free diet [N1-R3][N2-F2].

The evidence also supports that in some cases, a no-biopsy approach can reduce cost, risk, and caseload, but it does not substitute for traditional endoscopy and biopsy [N4-R4]. So the harm-minimization strategy is not to skip endoscopy entirely, but to do it carefully and with the best available evidence. In short, the best way to minimize harm is to delay a gluten-free trial and prioritize endoscopy and biopsy [N5-R1][N4-F3][N2-R2].

### Bottom line for the patient

Starting a gluten-free diet can destroy the diagnostic value of serology and may make biopsy less useful [N5-R1][N4-F3]. A trial is useful only when gluten intake has already been reduced or eliminated before definitive evaluation, but it is misleading if used as the first step in a patient with borderline serology [N2-R2][N1-F1]. To minimize harm, the patient should stay on gluten and be scheduled for endoscopy and biopsy as soon as possible [N4-F3]. The evidence supports a cautious, testing-first approach rather than an immediate gluten-free trial [N1-R3][N2-F2].

## Branch report: how to communicate uncertainty to the patient

### How to explain the risks of a lifelong diet change

The evidence makes it clear that a lifelong gluten-free diet is a major commitment and carries real risks if the diagnosis is uncertain. The evidence explicitly states that an incorrect diagnosis of celiac disease represents both a health risk for the patient and a risk to the healthcare system because of the necessity of a lifelong gluten-free diet [N5-R2]. It also notes that blood tests may not predict celiac disease in 100% of cases and that false positives can occur [N5-R3]. This means the patient should be told that a gluten-free diet is not a routine or reversible option; it is a lifelong change that should be made only when the diagnosis is sufficiently certain.

The evidence also warns that if a gluten-free diet has been started, antibody testing is not accurate [N5-R1]. This is important because it shows that the patient may be losing diagnostic information rather than gaining certainty. So the message should be: “A gluten-free diet is a serious lifelong commitment, and it can change the results of tests that would otherwise confirm or rule out celiac disease” [N5-R1][N5-R2].

### How to phrase next steps and shared decision-making

The evidence supports a shared decision-making approach. The guideline review says that discussing uncertainty is a critical element of shared decision-making [N6-R1]. The same source also says that various strategies can be used to minimize and manage uncertainty without eliminating it [N6-R3]. This means the clinician should present the options, the evidence, and the risks in plain language and invite the patient to participate in the decision.

The diagnostic pathway also emphasizes that serology is not sufficient on its own and that endoscopy and biopsy are the gold standard [N4-F3]. So the next steps should be framed as a diagnostic process rather than an immediate decision. The evidence also supports targeted testing, especially when serology is borderline [N1-F1]. This means the clinician should explain that the next step is to obtain more information before deciding whether to start a gluten-free diet [N2-F2][N4-F3].

### How to balance reassurance with caution

The evidence supports balancing reassurance with caution. The Mayo Clinic guidelines note that treatment for celiac disease is implementation of a gluten-free diet, but the evidence also emphasizes that serology is imperfect and can be misleading [N2-F2][N1-F1]. This means the clinician can reassure the patient that the symptoms may be consistent with celiac disease, but should also caution that the diagnosis is not certain and that the evidence is not strong enough to justify a lifelong diet immediately [N2-F2][N3-R2][N1-R3].

The communication evidence also says that effective communication about uncertainty is essential in medicine and that uncertainty should be discussed openly [N6-R2][N6-R3]. That means the clinician should be honest about what is known and what is not known, rather than giving false reassurance. At the same time, the evidence supports a practical pathway: keep the patient on gluten, schedule endoscopy and biopsy, and use serology with total IgA where needed [N2-F2][N4-F3]. This gives the patient a clear, evidence-based pathway that balances optimism about the possibility of celiac disease with caution about the need for testing before making a lifelong change [N1-F1][N4-F3].

### Bottom line for the patient

The patient should be told that a gluten-free diet is a major lifelong commitment and that starting it can change the results of tests that would otherwise confirm or rule out celiac disease [N5-R1][N5-R2]. The next steps should be framed as a diagnostic process: keep the patient on gluten, schedule endoscopy and biopsy, and use the best available serology with total IgA [N2-F2][N4-F3]. The message should balance reassurance that the symptoms may be consistent with celiac disease with caution that the diagnosis is not certain and that a gluten-free diet should not be assumed without stronger evidence [N2-F2][N1-F1].

### How likely true celiac disease is with borderline serology

The evidence strongly suggests that borderline serology is not a strong indicator of true celiac disease. The National Celiac Association states that a simple gliadin antibody test can be elevated in many conditions and should not be ordered on its own [N1-R3]. The broader diagnostic review also notes that serological testing has limited performance characteristics and that false positives can occur even with “borderline” results [N1-F1]. Several factors affect the threshold for diagnosis. The Mayo Clinic guidelines emphasize that TTG-IgA is the optimal initial test, and it should be used with total IgA to avoid false-negative results in IgA deficiency [N2-F2]. This means that the diagnostic threshold is not low; it is higher when the test is done properly with appropriate adjuncts. The review also explains that the positive predictive value of serology in the general population is low because of the high prevalence of undiagnosed celiac disease and imperfect specificity [N1-F1]. In practical terms, this means that the threshold for acting on a borderline result should be higher than on a clearly positive result. The evidence also supports a targeted approach rather than universal screening, especially when serology is borderline [N1-F1].

### Whether a gluten-free trial is defensible or should be delayed

A gluten-free trial is defensible only when the diagnostic uncertainty is high enough that the potential benefits of early treatment outweigh the risks of misdiagnosis. The evidence explicitly warns that an incorrect diagnosis of celiac disease represents a major health risk because of the necessity of a lifelong gluten-free diet [N5-R2]. It also says that if a gluten-free diet has been started, celiac antibody blood testing is not accurate [N5-R1]. This matters because a trial can destroy the diagnostic value of subsequent serology and biopsy.

The guidelines also note that gluten challenge is most commonly used when gluten intake has already been reduced or eliminated before definitive evaluation [N2-R2]. That means a gluten-free trial can be useful only in a narrow, well-defined setting. ### Bottom line for the patient

Borderline serology does not strongly support a gluten-free diet because it is not specific and can be misleading [N1-R3][N1-F1]. The threshold for diagnosis should be higher than for a clearly positive result, and the evidence supports using TTG-IgA with total IgA as the best initial approach [N2-F2].
